title: Future Tense
subtitle: Will, going to, and the one that looks like the present.
objectives: Form the future with will and with going to
Choose between will and going to
Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements

cards.eyebrow: Part 4 · What has not happened yet
cards.title: English has three ways of talking about the future
cards.text: And they are not interchangeable. The one you pick says how certain the thing is.

cards.title: For decisions made now, and predictions
cards.text: Will plus the base verb. No -s, no -ed, nothing.
points: **I will train tomorrow.** Decided as I speak.
**It will rain later.** A prediction.
**Never 'will trained' or 'will trains'.**
**Shortened to 'll** in speech: *I'll go*.

cards.title: For plans already made, and visible evidence
cards.text: Going to plus the base verb. The decision happened before now.
points: **I am going to replace the capacitor.** Already decided.
**Those clouds — it is going to rain.** The evidence is in front of you.
**Will** is the spur of the moment. **Going to** is the plan.
**Both are correct English.** They just mean slightly different things.

question.text: Your friend drops a glass. You say…
options: I am going to catch it.
question.explain: Decided this instant, with no prior plan. That is what 'will' is for.

cards.title: A flight plan is all 'going to'
cards.text: Nothing about a scheduled flight is decided on the spot.
points: **We are going to cruise at 35,000 feet.** Planned hours ago.
**The flight departs at 06:40.** A timetable, so present tense.
**'We will divert'** only if something unexpected happens.
**The grammar tracks** how fixed the plan is.

cards.title: The present continuous does future work
cards.text: When something is diarised, English often uses the -ing form.
points: **I am fighting on Saturday.** Already arranged.
**He is flying to Cebu on Monday.** Ticket booked.
**It sounds like the present** and means the future.
**Only for arrangements**, not predictions.

cards.title: A fight camp runs on 'going to'
cards.text: Everything in a camp is planned weeks out. Almost nothing about it is decided in the moment.
points: **I am going to cut weight** over the next three weeks.
**He is fighting on the 14th.** Arranged, so present continuous.
**'I will stop' is what you say** when your body decides for you.
**The grammar shows** what was planned and what was not.

question.text: 'I will going to train' is correct English.
question.explain: It mixes two future forms. Pick one: 'I will train' or 'I am going to train'.

cards.title: Literature Review: Don Quixote, Chapter 14: The Message to Dulcinea
cards.text: Sancho is sent to deliver a letter to a lady who does not know she is a lady.
points: **'I will take it,'** says Sancho, deciding on the spot.
**He is going to invent** most of what he reports back.
**He never delivers it.** He loses the letter.
**Promises about the future** run all through the chapter.

question.text: Which shows a plan made earlier?
options: I am going to fix it.
question.explain: 'Going to' signals the decision was already taken. 'Will' would mean deciding now.

terms.def: The future form for decisions made now and for predictions.
The future form for existing plans and visible evidence.
The -ing form, used for fixed future arrangements.
The plain verb with no ending.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Will: decided now, or a prediction.
Going to: already planned, or the evidence is visible.
Am/is/are + -ing: a fixed arrangement.
Never mix two future forms in one verb.

quiz.explain: Will takes the base verb, with nothing added.
quiz.objective: Form the future with will and with going to

quiz.explain: The evidence is in front of you, which is what 'going to' is for.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 4 English. The three future forms are taught by what they imply rather than as interchangeable options, because choosing between will and going to is the actual skill and most learners treat them as synonyms. The dropped-glass example gives 'will' its clearest use — a decision made in the moment — and the flight plan gives 'going to' its clearest one. The present continuous is included because it is extremely common in speech and is otherwise baffling: a present-looking form that means the future. The mixed form 'will going to' gets a direct checkpoint.
discussion: What is the difference between 'I will fix it' and 'I am going to fix it'?
Why does a flight plan never use 'will'?
How can a present-tense form mean the future?
extension: Write five sentences about next week using all three forms correctly.
Listen for 'going to' in conversation and note whether a plan existed.
misconceptions: Treating will and going to as identical.
